nameStory: The pea hawthorn gets its name from its small, pea-sized fruits that ripen in late summer. Unlike many of its hawthorn cousins that produce larger, more apple-like fruits, this species keeps things petite with berries that could easily be mistaken for tiny peas hanging from the branches. The scientific name 'pisifera' literally means 'pea-bearing' in Latin, making this one of the more straightforward plant names you'll encounter!
description: Pea hawthorn is a small to medium-sized shrub or small tree in the rose family, typically growing 10-20 feet tall. Like all hawthorns, it's armed with sharp thorns along its branches and produces clusters of small white flowers in spring. The plant has a somewhat scraggly, irregular growth habit with dense branching. Its most distinctive feature is its unusually small fruits compared to other hawthorns, earning it the 'pea' part of its common name.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny round fruits, truly pea-sized at about 1/4 inch across, that ripen to dark red or purple-black in late summer. They feel firm and have a slightly waxy surface when rubbed between your fingers.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers with 5 petals arranged in flat-topped clusters in May. The flowers have a faint, sweet rose-like fragrance and numerous stamens that give them a fuzzy appearance in the center.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval to egg-shaped leaves with shallow lobes or large teeth along the edges. They feel somewhat thick and leathery to the touch, with a smooth, glossy upper surface that catches the light.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Grayish-brown bark that becomes scaly with age, flaking off in small irregular patches. On younger branches, the bark feels smooth but is interrupted by sharp thorns up to 2 inches long.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a small tree or large shrub with an open, somewhat irregular crown. Branches have a zigzag pattern and are densely armed with long, straight thorns that are sharp enough to pierce clothing.

habitat: Pea hawthorn prefers open, sunny locations with well-drained soils, often found along forest edges, old fields, and roadside thickets. In New England, it's most commonly encountered in areas that have been disturbed or cleared, as it's an early colonizer of abandoned farmland. It tolerates a variety of soil types but seems to favor slightly alkaline conditions.

seasonality.spring: White flower clusters bloom in May, creating fragrant displays that attract bees and other pollinators. New leaves emerge bright green and have a fresh, slightly glossy appearance.
seasonality.summer: Leaves are fully developed and dark green, while small green fruits begin forming and gradually enlarge. This is when the thorns are most noticeable as they're not hidden by fall colors or bare winter branches.
seasonality.fall: The tiny pea-sized fruits ripen to dark red or purple-black and may persist into early winter. Leaves turn yellow to orange-red before dropping, making the thorny branch structure more visible.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the plant's thorny, zigzag branching pattern. Some dark fruits may still cling to branches, and the scaly bark becomes more apparent without leaf cover.

funFact: Despite being called 'pea hawthorn,' the tiny fruits are actually more closely related to miniature apples than peas! Like all hawthorns, each little fruit contains 1-3 hard seeds and belongs to the same plant subfamily as apples and pears, making every berry a microscopic version of your favorite orchard fruit.
confusionNotes: Pea hawthorn can be confused with other small-fruited hawthorns, but its exceptionally tiny fruits are the key distinguishing feature - if you're holding what looks like an actual pea rather than a small cherry, you've likely found pea hawthorn. Remember: 'pea-sized means pea hawthorn' to distinguish it from the larger-fruited species in the genus.
contextualKnowledge: Hawthorns as a group are notoriously difficult to identify, with botanists recognizing dozens of species that often hybridize and show variable characteristics. Pea hawthorn is actually one of the easier ones to identify precisely because of its distinctively small fruit size, making it a good 'starter hawthorn' for beginning botanists.
compareHints: Among New England's hawthorns, pea hawthorn stands out for having the smallest fruits in the genus - significantly smaller than the cherry-sized fruits of dotted hawthorn or the larger berries of cockspur hawthorn. While most hawthorns have fruits ranging from 1/3 to 3/4 inch across, pea hawthorn's fruits are consistently under 1/4 inch. The thorns are also notably long and straight compared to some other species that have shorter or more curved spines.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Dotted hawthorn stands out from its many New England relatives primarily by its spotted fruits.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, common hawthorn stands out for having just one seed per fruit (most others have 2-5 seeds) and deeply lobed leaves with 3-7 divisions.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, cockspur stands out with the longest thorns - much longer than dotted hawthorn's short spines or Washington hawthorn's modest thorns.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, big-fruit hawthorn stands out for its notably larger berries and earlier bloom time.
Among New England hawthorns, large-thorn hawthorn stands out primarily for its exceptionally long, straight thorns that dwarf those of relatives like dotted hawthorn or common hawthorn.

Among the many hawthorn species in New England, Washington hawthorn stands out with its distinctly triangular, deeply lobed leaves (rather than the more oval or rounded leaves of species like dotted hawthorn).
Among New England's many hawthorn species, waxy-fruited hawthorn stands out primarily for its distinctively coated berries - no other local hawthorn has that waxy, frosted appearance on the fruits.

Among New England's many hawthorns, fireberry hawthorn stands out for its golden-yellow unripe fruits - most relatives like dotted hawthorn or cockspur hawthorn have green unripe fruits that turn red.
Large-flowered cockspurthorn stands out from its many hawthorn relatives primarily by its notably large flowers - nearly twice the size of most other hawthorns.
Among New England hawthorns, fanleaf hawthorn is distinguished by its broader, more fan-shaped leaves compared to most relatives.
Among New England hawthorns, Biltmore hawthorn stands out for its green, yellow, or orange fruits - most others like dotted hawthorn, common hawthorn, and cockspur hawthorn have red fruits.

Cleft-leaved hawthorn's leaves are much more deeply divided than most New England hawthorns - while dotted hawthorn has shallow lobes and cockspur hawthorn has barely any lobes at all, this species' leaves are cut nearly to the midrib.
Among New England's many hawthorns, downy hawthorn stands out for its distinctly fuzzy leaf undersides - most others like dotted hawthorn or common hawthorn have smooth or only slightly hairy leaves.
Blanchard's hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having more deeply lobed leaves and longer thorns.
Miss Jones' hawthorn is distinguished from other New England hawthorns primarily by subtle differences in leaf shape, thorn characteristics, and fruit details that require close examination.
Stone's hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having more deeply lobed leaves and different fruit characteristics.
Fleshy hawthorn stands out from its many hawthorn relatives by having the juiciest, most succulent berries in the group.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, scarlet hawthorn is distinguished by its particularly prominent thorns and bright red fruits.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, Schuette's hawthorn is distinguished by subtle characteristics that require expert identification.
Northern hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having less deeply lobed leaves and different fruit characteristics, though these distinctions can be subtle.
Dodge's hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having less prominently marked leaves and typically fewer, larger thorns.
Holmes' hawthorn is most closely related to scarlet hawthorn but distinguished by its more elongated leaves and egg-shaped rather than round fruits.
Among New England's many hawthorns, broad-leaved cockspurthorn stands out for its exceptionally broad, substantial leaves that are wider than most of its relatives.
Hairy cockspurthorn differs from its closest relative, downy hawthorn, primarily in having about 10 stamens per flower instead of 20, and the two species have separate native ranges.

Grove hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having longer thorns and less deeply cut leaves.
Keep's Hawthorn differs from common hawthorns like dotted hawthorn in subtle leaf lobe patterns and fruit characteristics that require expert knowledge to distinguish reliably.

Among New England hawthorns, poplar hawthorn stands out immediately for its broad, oval, relatively unlobed leaves - most other hawthorns like dotted hawthorn or common hawthorn have deeply cut, lobed leaves.
Unlike the common red-fruited hawthorns like dotted hawthorn or cockspur hawthorn, straw-fruited hawthorn produces distinctively pale yellow berries.

Among New England's many hawthorn species, stinking hawthorn stands out for its yellow-green fruits with red markings rather than the solid red fruits of most others like dotted hawthorn or cockspur hawthorn.
